newsitem.title: USA: Strong dlr no substitute for rate hike - Fed source.
newsitem.headline: Strong dlr no substitute for rate hike - Fed source.

text.p: The rising dollar is no substitute for tighter monetary policy if economic conditions warrant higher short-term interest rates, a source close to the Federal Reserve told Reuters.

"The fact the dollar has been appreciating would not stop a tightening if the Fed were to see a need to do so," the source said, adding that wage-related inflationary pressures remain the focus of the central bank's vigilance.
"A rising dollar is no substitute for higher interest rates," the source said.

"The dollar is one factor among many" that the Fed uses to determine policy, the source added, reiterating the view expressed by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan in recent testimony before the Senate banking committee.

Greenspan said the dollar "almost never" is the key to determining interest rates. Indeed, the Fed has not cited the dollar as a factor in monetary policy since 1979. The 1985 Plaza Accord that lowered the dollar and the 1987 Le Louvre Accord that stabilized it were not accompanied by monetary policy changes.
Stephen Axilrod, former Fed Staff Director and FOMC Secretary agreed that "the dollar is a very, very minor factor" in Fed policy.

"The dominant factor is whether there is enough inflationary pressure percolating in the system," added Axilrod, an advisor at MFR Inc who took part in the Plaza Accord of 1985. "The dollar is at best a marginal factor in the thinking at the Fed."
Minutes of Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings, where the Fed sets monetary policy, generally contain only very brief mentions of the dollar, the source noted.

The latest available FOMC minutes, for the November 13, 1996 meeting, summarize foreign exchange developments with the brief note that the dollar "rose against the yen as prospects for a significant supplemental budget package in Japan waned."
Main FOMC references to the dollar in 1996 -- a year when the U.S. currency rose by about 11.5 percent versus the yen -- were made at the January 30-31 and May 21 meetings.

"The recent appreciation in the foreign exchange markets also might tend to damp net exports. Consequently, several members saw downside risks in the foreign trade sector over the year ahead," the FOMC said in late January 1996.
That reference followed a 5.7-percent surge in dollar/yen between mid-November 1995 and late January 1996.

The FOMC also noted in May 1996 "the appreciation of the dollar over the past year and near-term moderation in federal government spending also were expected to exert some restraint on economic activity over the forecast horizon."
Dollar/yen appreciated by 22.7 percent in the year preceeding the May 1996 meeting, in a rebound from the post-War low set on April 19, 1995 at 79.75.
The FOMC lowered short-term rates in January 1996, its last easing, and left rates unchanged in May of last year.

The dollar has surged by about 7.0 percent against the yen since the last FOMC meeting on December 17. This could help reduce inflation concerns by making imports less costly when paid for in dollars, according to some market analysts.
San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry recently noted that a strong dollar is "a factor that maybe keeps a little bit of downward pressure on inflation."
Some U.S. business leaders have complained about Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's statements that a strong dollar is in the U.S. interest.
"A strong dollar helps us to keep interest rates down, helps to keep inflation down," Rubin told Reuters in November.
But Economic Strategy Institute chief economist Lawrence Chimerine said "the fact is the higher dollar has a very limited effect on interest rates in the United States."
"The way for foreign countries to stimulate their economy is not by letting them export more to the United States while we already have large trade deficits," he added.
